acceptedAnswer.text: Multithreading in Java is the ability to execute multiple threads concurrently within a single Java process. A thread is the smallest unit of execution — it has its own program counter, stack, and local variables, but shares the heap memory (objects, static fields) with all other threads in the same process. Multithreading enables: parallel processing on multi-core CPUs, responsive UIs (keeping the UI thread free while background tasks run), efficient I/O handling (serving thousands of HTTP requests simultaneously), and better CPU utilisation when tasks are I/O-bound.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between Thread class and Runnable interface in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: Thread is a class — extending it creates a thread but consumes the single inheritance slot. Runnable is a functional interface with a single run() method — implementing it separates the task from the thread mechanism, allows the class to extend another class, and lets the same Runnable be submitted to thread pools, executors, or virtual threads. Preference: always prefer Runnable (or Callable for results) over extending Thread. Thread extension is only justified when you need to override other Thread methods like interrupt handling.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between synchronized method and synchronized block?

acceptedAnswer.text: A synchronized method acquires the lock on 'this' (for instance methods) or the Class object (for static methods) for the entire method duration. A synchronized block acquires a lock on a specified object for only the block's duration — enabling finer-grained locking. Synchronized blocks are preferred because: (1) smaller critical section = less lock contention = better throughput, (2) you can choose any object as the lock (not just 'this'), (3) different locks can protect different data, allowing concurrent access to independent state.

mainEntity.name: What is a deadlock in Java? How do you prevent it?

acceptedAnswer.text: A deadlock is a situation where two or more threads are permanently blocked waiting for locks held by each other. Thread A holds Lock 1 and waits for Lock 2; Thread B holds Lock 2 and waits for Lock 1 — neither can proceed. Prevention strategies: (1) Lock ordering — always acquire locks in the same global order across all threads. (2) Lock timeout — use tryLock(timeout) from ReentrantLock instead of blocking indefinitely. (3) Avoid nested locking — minimise holding multiple locks simultaneously. (4) Use higher-level concurrency utilities (java.util.concurrent) that handle locking internally.

mainEntity.name: What are virtual threads in Java 21?

acceptedAnswer.text: Virtual threads (Project Loom, standard in Java 21) are lightweight threads managed by the JVM rather than the OS. Traditional platform threads map 1:1 to OS threads — expensive to create (1MB+ stack), limiting applications to thousands of concurrent threads. Virtual threads are mounted on a small pool of carrier threads and unmounted during blocking I/O — allowing millions of concurrent virtual threads with minimal memory overhead. Virtual threads are ideal for high-throughput server applications with many concurrent I/O-bound tasks. Create them with: Thread.ofVirtual().start(runnable) or Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor().

sections.title: What is Multithreading in Java?

blocks.text: Multithreading is the ability of a Java program to execute multiple threads simultaneously within a single process. A thread is the smallest unit of CPU execution — it has its own program counter, call stack, and local variables, but shares the heap memory (objects, static fields, open files) with all other threads in the same JVM process. This shared memory is what makes threads powerful and dangerous at the same time.

Modern applications are inherently concurrent. A web server handles thousands of HTTP requests simultaneously — each on its own thread. A payment gateway processes multiple transactions in parallel. A trading platform ticks market prices while executing orders concurrently. An IDE compiles code in the background while you keep typing. Without multithreading, none of these systems would scale.

The two primary benefits of multithreading are: (1) CPU utilisation — on a multi-core processor, threads run truly in parallel across cores, multiplying throughput. (2) Responsiveness — the UI thread stays free while a background thread does heavy computation or waits for I/O. The primary risk is shared mutable state — when two threads simultaneously read and write the same object without coordination, the result is unpredictable: race conditions, stale data, and corruption.

blocks.title: 🔑 Java Multithreading at a Glance
blocks.text: Key concepts: (1) Thread / Runnable — two ways to define a task. (2) Thread Lifecycle — NEW → RUNNABLE → RUNNING → BLOCKED/WAITING → TERMINATED. (3) synchronized — mutual exclusion via monitor locks. (4) volatile — visibility guarantee across threads. (5) wait()/notify() — thread-to-thread communication via shared object monitor. (6) Executor Framework — manages thread pools; never create raw Thread in production. (7) Callable/Future — threads that return results and handle exceptions. (8) CompletableFuture — non-blocking async pipelines. (9) Atomic classes — lock-free thread safety for single variables. (10) Virtual Threads (Java 21) — millions of lightweight threads for I/O-bound workloads.

sections.title: Creating Threads — Thread Class vs Runnable Interface

blocks.text: Java provides two classic ways to define a concurrent task: extending Thread and implementing Runnable. A third way — implementing Callable — is used when the task must return a result or throw a checked exception. In modern Java, lambdas make Runnable and Callable extremely concise, and the Executor framework manages the actual threads — raw Thread creation is reserved for low-level scenarios.

blocks.title: ⚠️ Always Call start(), Never run() Directly
blocks.text: Calling thread.run() does NOT start a new thread — it executes the run() method on the CURRENT thread synchronously, like a normal method call. Only thread.start() tells the JVM to create a new OS thread, schedule it, and call run() on that new thread. Calling start() twice on the same Thread object throws IllegalThreadStateException — a Thread can only be started once. Create a new Thread instance if you need to run the task again.

blocks.title: ⚠️ Never Swallow InterruptedException
blocks.text: The single most common threading mistake: catching InterruptedException and doing nothing. When you catch InterruptedException, the thread's interrupt flag is cleared. If you don't re-interrupt the thread (Thread.currentThread().interrupt()) or rethrow the exception, the interruption is permanently lost — any code up the call stack that checks isInterrupted() will see false and never know a shutdown was requested. Rule: either rethrow the exception, or re-interrupt the thread before returning from the catch block.

sections.title: Synchronization — Preventing Race Conditions

blocks.text: A race condition occurs when two or more threads access shared mutable data concurrently and the outcome depends on the unpredictable order of their execution. Java's primary tool to prevent race conditions is synchronization — built around the concept of a monitor lock (also called an intrinsic lock). Every Java object has exactly one monitor lock. The synchronized keyword causes a thread to acquire the lock before entering a block or method, and release it upon exit — ensuring only one thread at a time executes the guarded code.

Simple to write but coarser-grained — any caller must wait even if it only needs to read an unrelated field. Two synchronized instance methods on the SAME object cannot run concurrently.

sections.title: volatile Keyword — Visibility Guarantee Without Mutual Exclusion

blocks.text: The volatile keyword solves a specific problem: memory visibility. Without volatile, each CPU core may cache a thread's local copy of a variable in its registers or L1/L2 cache. A write by Thread A may not be visible to Thread B running on a different core for an unpredictable amount of time. volatile guarantees that every read of a volatile variable goes to main memory, and every write immediately flushes to main memory — establishing a happens-before relationship.

sections.title: wait(), notify(), notifyAll() — Thread Communication

blocks.text: While synchronized prevents two threads from running simultaneously, wait() and notify() allow threads to coordinate — one thread can pause and wait for a condition to be met, while another thread signals that the condition has changed. This is the classic Producer-Consumer coordination pattern. All three methods (wait, notify, notifyAll) must be called inside a synchronized block on the same object — the monitor object.

blocks.title: ⚠️ Always use while Loop — Never if — Around wait()
blocks.text: A waiting thread can wake up spuriously (without notify() being called) — this is allowed by the Java specification. If you use 'if (condition) wait()', a spurious wakeup proceeds without re-checking the condition, potentially operating on invalid state. Always use 'while (condition) wait()' — after every wakeup (spurious or real), the condition is re-evaluated. This is one of the most important and most commonly violated rules of wait/notify programming.

sections.title: Executor Framework — Thread Pools Done Right

blocks.text: Creating a raw new Thread() for every task is dangerous in production: thread creation is expensive (1–10ms), unbounded thread creation exhausts OS resources, and there is no lifecycle management. The Executor framework (java.util.concurrent) solves all of this — it manages a pool of reusable threads, queues tasks, handles thread lifecycle, and provides controlled shutdown. ExecutorService is the interface; Executors factory class creates common pool configurations.

blocks.title: 💡 Rejection Policies — What Happens When the Queue is Full
blocks.text: When a ThreadPoolExecutor's queue is full AND all threads are busy, it applies a RejectionPolicy: AbortPolicy (default) — throws RejectedExecutionException. CallerRunsPolicy — runs the task on the calling thread (provides backpressure, slows the submitter). DiscardPolicy — silently drops the task. DiscardOldestPolicy — drops the oldest queued task and retries submission. In production APIs, CallerRunsPolicy is often the safest choice — it prevents data loss while creating natural back-pressure to slow inbound traffic.

sections.title: Callable & Future — Threads That Return Results

blocks.text: Runnable.run() returns void and cannot throw checked exceptions — it provides no way to get a result back from a thread. Callable<V> solves both problems: its call() method returns a typed value V and can throw any checked exception. When submitted to an ExecutorService, it returns a Future<V> — a handle to the computation that lets you check completion, retrieve the result, cancel the task, or handle exceptions.

sections.title: Atomic Classes — Lock-Free Thread Safety

blocks.text: The java.util.concurrent.atomic package provides thread-safe classes for single-variable operations without locks. They use Compare-And-Swap (CAS) — a CPU-level instruction that atomically reads, compares, and writes a value only if it still matches the expected value. This is faster than synchronised methods for simple operations because there is no lock contention, no context switch, and no thread blocking.

sections.title: Deadlock — Detection, Prevention & Resolution

blocks.text: A deadlock is one of the most feared concurrency bugs — a situation where two or more threads are permanently blocked, each waiting for a resource held by another. The JVM does not automatically detect or resolve deadlocks (unlike databases). A deadlocked application simply hangs — no error, no log, no recovery — making it extremely hard to diagnose in production.

items.title: Four Conditions for Deadlock (Coffman)
items.text:
ALL four must hold simultaneously for deadlock to occur:
1. Mutual Exclusion — resources can only be held by one thread.
2. Hold and Wait — a thread holds one resource while waiting for another.
3. No Preemption — a resource cannot be forcibly taken from a thread.
4. Circular Wait — Thread A waits for Thread B, Thread B waits for Thread A.
Breaking ANY one condition prevents deadlock.

items.title: Prevention Strategy 1: Lock Ordering
items.text:
Always acquire multiple locks in the SAME GLOBAL ORDER across ALL threads.
Bad: Thread A acquires Lock1 then Lock2; Thread B acquires Lock2 then Lock1.
Good: Both threads always acquire Lock1 first, then Lock2.
This breaks Circular Wait — deadlock is impossible when all threads agree on lock order.
For locks on domain objects, use a consistent ordering like object hash code or ID.

items.title: Prevention Strategy 2: tryLock with Timeout
items.text:
Use ReentrantLock.tryLock(timeout) instead of synchronized or lock.lock().
If the lock isn't available within the timeout, back off, release all held locks, and retry later.
This breaks Hold-and-Wait — a thread that can't get all locks releases what it has.
Java thread dumps (jstack) and VisualVM show BLOCKED threads — useful for detecting deadlock in production.

sections.title: Virtual Threads — Project Loom (Java 21)

blocks.text: Virtual threads are the most significant concurrency feature added to Java in two decades, standardised in Java 21 (JEP 444). Traditional platform threads map 1:1 to OS threads — each consumes roughly 1–2 MB of stack memory and is expensive to create and context-switch. Applications serving 10,000 concurrent connections needed 10,000 OS threads, which is impractical. Virtual threads are managed entirely by the JVM — they are mounted on a small pool of underlying OS threads (carrier threads) and automatically unmounted when they block on I/O, freeing the carrier thread for another virtual thread.

items.title: Platform Thread (Traditional)
items.text:
Backed by an OS thread.
Stack: 512KB – 2MB per thread.
OS thread limit: typically ~thousands per JVM.
Creation: slow (~1ms, system call required).
Blocking I/O: OS thread is blocked — carrier thread occupied.
Cost: expensive — thread pool required to manage lifecycle.
Best for: CPU-bound tasks, low-concurrency scenarios.

items.title: Virtual Thread (Java 21+)
items.text:
Backed by JVM-managed carrier threads (ForkJoinPool).
Stack: starts at ~KB, grows lazily on heap.
Capacity: MILLIONS per JVM.
Creation: fast — no OS system call.
Blocking I/O: virtual thread unmounted from carrier — carrier free for others.
Cost: cheap — create one per task (no pooling needed).
Best for: I/O-bound tasks, high-concurrency server applications.

items.title: Virtual Thread Caveats
items.text:
1. Pinning: a virtual thread is 'pinned' to its carrier if it holds a synchronized lock during I/O — blocking the carrier. Fix: replace synchronized with ReentrantLock inside code that does blocking I/O.
2. Thread-local variables: ThreadLocal with large values multiplied by millions of virtual threads = memory pressure. Consider alternatives.
3. Not for CPU-bound work: virtual threads don't add CPU parallelism — use ForkJoinPool/parallelStream for parallel computation.
4. Still in adaptation: many libraries need updates to use non-pinning I/O.

sections.title: Common Mistakes & Pitfalls — Bugs That Fool Everyone

blocks.text: Concurrency bugs are among the most insidious in software engineering — they are often non-deterministic, appear only under load, and vanish when you add logging or a debugger. These are the patterns that fill production incident reports.

sections.title: Bad Practices & Anti-Patterns — What Senior Developers Reject

blocks.text: These concurrency anti-patterns are the most common causes of production incidents, performance degradation, and system instability in Java applications.

items.title: Thread-Per-Request Without Limits (Thread Bomb)
items.text: Spawning a new thread for every incoming request without any limit — whether via raw Thread creation or an unbounded CachedThreadPool — will exhaust OS thread limits under load. Each OS thread costs 512KB–2MB of stack. 10,000 requests = 10,000 threads = 10GB RAM for stacks alone. Use a bounded thread pool (ThreadPoolExecutor with bounded queue and CallerRunsPolicy) or virtual threads. Always design for the worst-case request concurrency.

items.title: Excessive Synchronization (Lock Granularity Too Coarse)
items.text: Synchronising entire methods or large blocks when only a few lines access shared state serialises all callers, eliminating concurrency benefits. Example: synchronizing a method that does 1000ms of computation to protect a 1ms counter update. Fix: use fine-grained locks covering only the critical section; use read/write locks when reads vastly outnumber writes; use atomic classes for single-variable updates.

items.title: Ignoring Thread Pool Saturation
items.text: Submitting tasks to an executor without handling RejectedExecutionException or ignoring task queue depth. When the queue fills and all threads are busy, the default AbortPolicy silently discards tasks. In a payment or order system, this causes silent data loss. Always choose a RejectionPolicy deliberately, monitor queue depth with pool.getQueue().size(), and alert or back-pressure when saturation is detected.

items.title: Using Deprecated Thread Methods (stop, suspend, resume)
items.text: Thread.stop() forcibly kills a thread while it holds locks — leaving shared objects in inconsistent state. Thread.suspend() holds locks while suspended — classic deadlock trigger. Both are deprecated since Java 1.2. Never use them. Use volatile flags, interrupt(), and cooperative shutdown patterns instead. The Java specification explicitly warns that these methods are fundamentally unsafe.

items.title: Sharing ThreadLocal State Across a Thread Pool
items.text: ThreadLocal stores per-thread data. In a thread pool, threads are reused — a ThreadLocal value set by one task is visible to the next task running on the same thread if it isn't cleared. This causes request context leakage: user A's authentication context leaking into user B's request is a security incident. Always call ThreadLocal.remove() in a finally block after the task completes when using thread pools.

items.title: Busy-Waiting (Polling in a Tight Loop)
items.text: while (!ready) {} — a busy-wait loop burns 100% CPU on a core doing nothing useful, and due to memory visibility rules, may loop forever without volatile. Use proper blocking mechanisms: CountDownLatch.await(), BlockingQueue.take(), CompletableFuture.join(), or wait()/notify(). Busy-waiting is only ever justified in very tight latency-sensitive lock-free algorithms, and even then with Thread.onSpinWait() hints to the CPU.

sections.title: Java Multithreading Interview Questions — Beginner to Advanced

blocks.text: These questions are consistently asked in Java backend, system design, and senior developer interviews — covering both conceptual understanding and practical debugging skills.

items.q: Q1. What is the difference between Process and Thread in Java?
items.a: A Process is an independent program in execution with its own isolated memory space, file handles, and OS resources. Processes communicate via IPC (sockets, pipes, shared memory). A Thread is a lightweight unit of execution within a process — it shares the process's heap, static variables, and open files with other threads, but has its own stack, program counter, and local variables. Creating a thread is much cheaper than creating a process (~microseconds vs milliseconds). In a Java JVM, you have one process containing multiple threads. Inter-thread communication is fast (shared heap) but dangerous (race conditions). Inter-process communication is safe (isolated) but expensive.

items.q: Q2. What is a race condition? Give a concrete Java example.
items.a: A race condition occurs when the correctness of a program depends on the relative timing of thread execution. Example: two threads increment a shared 'counter' variable. counter++ is not atomic — it expands to: (1) read counter, (2) add 1, (3) write counter. If Thread A reads counter=5 and Thread B also reads counter=5 before either writes, both compute 6 and write 6 — the counter ends at 6 instead of 7 (lost update). Fix: use synchronized, AtomicInteger.incrementAndGet(), or LongAdder — all of which make the read-modify-write sequence atomic.

items.q: Q3. What is the difference between synchronized method and synchronized block?
items.a: synchronized method: acquires the monitor lock on 'this' (instance) or the Class object (static) for the entire method duration. All code in the method is in the critical section — even code that doesn't need protection. synchronized block: acquires a lock on a specified object for only the block's duration. You choose what to lock and how much code is protected. Advantages of blocks: (1) smaller critical section = less contention = higher throughput, (2) can lock on an object other than 'this' — prevents clients from interfering with your lock, (3) different locks for independent data allow concurrent access to unrelated state.

items.q: Q4. What is the difference between sleep() and wait()?
items.a: Thread.sleep(ms): a static method on Thread. Pauses the current thread for a specified time. Does NOT release any locks the thread holds. The thread wakes automatically after the time. Used for delays and polling. obj.wait(): an instance method on Object. Must be called inside synchronized(obj). Releases the monitor lock on obj and suspends the thread. The thread wakes when another thread calls obj.notify() or obj.notifyAll(). Used for thread coordination (producer-consumer). Key difference: sleep holds locks; wait releases them. sleep is a timer; wait is a coordination mechanism.

items.q: Q5. What is a deadlock? How do you detect and prevent it?
items.a: Deadlock: two or more threads permanently blocked, each waiting for a lock held by the other. Detection: jstack <pid> shows thread dumps — deadlocked threads appear in a BLOCKED cycle with 'waiting to lock' annotations. VisualVM, JConsole, and Java Flight Recorder also detect deadlocks. Prevention: (1) Lock ordering — always acquire locks in the same global order. (2) tryLock with timeout — release held locks if you can't get all. (3) Avoid holding multiple locks. (4) Use java.util.concurrent utilities that handle locking internally (ConcurrentHashMap, BlockingQueue). Resolution: in production, if detected — restart the service (deadlocks rarely self-resolve).

items.q: Q6. What is the volatile keyword in Java? What does it and does NOT guarantee?
items.a: volatile guarantees: (1) VISIBILITY — every read of a volatile variable reads from main memory; every write immediately flushes to main memory. A thread will always see the latest value written by any other thread. (2) ORDERING — establishes happens-before relationships, preventing instruction reordering around volatile reads/writes. volatile does NOT guarantee: ATOMICITY of compound operations. volatile int count; count++ is NOT atomic — it is still read-modify-write which can interleave between threads. Use AtomicInteger for atomic compound operations, or synchronized. volatile is correct for single-write, multi-read flags (boolean shutdown flag) and double-checked locking.

items.q: Q7. What is the Executor framework? Why should you never use raw Thread in production?
items.a: The Executor framework (java.util.concurrent) provides: managed thread pools (reuse threads, avoid creation overhead), task queuing, lifecycle management (shutdown/awaitTermination), and Future/CompletableFuture for result handling. Raw Thread problems: (1) creating a thread per request exhausts OS limits under load — threads are expensive (1–2MB stack each). (2) No lifecycle management — orphaned threads keep JVM running. (3) No rejection handling — unbounded thread creation. (4) Cannot return results or handle exceptions cleanly. Production standard: use ThreadPoolExecutor with tuned core/max/queue/rejection policy, or virtual thread executor (Java 21).

items.q: Q8. What is the difference between Callable and Runnable?
items.a: Runnable: functional interface with void run() — no return value, cannot throw checked exceptions. Used with Thread or ExecutorService.submit(). Callable<V>: functional interface with V call() throws Exception — returns a typed value, can throw any checked exception. Used with ExecutorService.submit() which returns Future<V>. When to use Callable: (1) task produces a result that you need (price calculation, data fetch), (2) task may throw a checked exception that should propagate to the caller, (3) you need to cancel the task or check if it's done via Future. CompletableFuture.supplyAsync() is the modern alternative to Callable+Future for non-blocking async pipelines.

items.q: Q9. What is CompletableFuture and how does it differ from Future?
items.a: Future (Java 5): represents a pending result. get() blocks the calling thread until done — it is a synchronous wait dressed up as async. Cannot chain transformations, handle errors elegantly, or combine multiple futures without blocking code. CompletableFuture (Java 8): supports non-blocking async pipelines via callbacks. thenApply() transforms the result without blocking. thenCompose() chains async operations (flatMap). thenCombine() merges two independent futures. exceptionally() handles errors. allOf()/anyOf() coordinate multiple futures. The calling thread is never blocked unless you explicitly call join() or get(). Enables reactive-style programming in Java without a reactive framework.

items.q: Q10. What are virtual threads (Project Loom) in Java 21 and when should you use them?
items.a: Virtual threads (JEP 444, Java 21) are JVM-managed lightweight threads that are not backed by OS threads 1:1. They are mounted on carrier threads (a small ForkJoinPool) and automatically unmounted during blocking I/O — freeing the carrier for other virtual threads. This allows millions of concurrent virtual threads with minimal memory overhead. Use when: serving high concurrency I/O-bound workloads (HTTP servers, DB queries, external APIs) where traditional thread pools bottleneck. Do NOT use for: CPU-bound work (virtual threads don't add CPU parallelism), code with heavily synchronized blocks on I/O paths (causes pinning — blocks the carrier). Migrate by replacing Executors.newFixedThreadPool() with Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor().

Fix: declare 'static volatile boolean flag = false'. The volatile keyword guarantees that every read of flag goes to main memory and every write is immediately visible to all threads. Deadlock: T1 acquires lock1 and waits for lock2. T2 acquires lock2 and waits for lock1. Neither can proceed — circular wait. Fix 1 (lock ordering): always acquire in the same order in both threads: synchronized(lock1) { synchronized(lock2) { ... } } in BOTH t1 AND t2. Lock1 is always acquired before lock2 globally — circular wait is impossible. Fix 2 (tryLock): use ReentrantLock.tryLock(timeout) in both threads — if a thread can't get both locks within the timeout, it releases what it has and retries. Fix 3: avoid nested locking altogether by restructuring the logic to require only one lock at a time.

7. What is thread starvation? How can it happen even without deadlock? Write a scenario.
items.a: Thread starvation is when a thread is perpetually denied CPU time or a lock, even though it is not deadlocked. It can make forward progress but is never scheduled. Scenario: ExecutorService with 2 threads. A high-priority long-running task is continuously submitted and always occupies both threads. A low-priority task is queued but never gets a turn because the queue always has higher-priority work ahead. Code: ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(2); // Thread A and Thread B forever loop submitting 5-second tasks — a short task submitted later waits forever. Fix: (1) Use a fair ThreadPoolExecutor with bounded queue. (2) Ensure long-running tasks don't monopolise threads. (3) Set task time limits. (4) Use separate pools for long-running and short-lived tasks. (5) ReentrantLock(true) — fair mode — prevents lock starvation by giving waiting threads turns in order.

sections.title: Conclusion — Multithreading: The Engine Behind Every High-Performance Java Application

blocks.text: Multithreading is where Java's true power manifests — and where its most subtle bugs hide. Every high-performance Java application, from a REST API serving thousands of concurrent users to a trading platform processing millions of events per second, relies on carefully designed concurrency. The raw mechanisms (Thread, synchronized, wait/notify) give you full control; the high-level abstractions (ExecutorService, CompletableFuture, ConcurrentHashMap) give you safety and productivity.

The hallmark of a senior Java engineer in concurrent programming: they never create raw threads in production code, they understand memory visibility as deeply as mutual exclusion, they know when volatile is sufficient and when synchronized is necessary, they design for graceful shutdown from day one, they choose CompletableFuture pipelines over blocking Future.get(), and in Java 21 applications they reach for virtual threads first for I/O-bound concurrency.

items.q: What is multithreading in Java?
items.a: Multithreading in Java is the ability to execute multiple threads concurrently within a single JVM process. Threads share the process heap (objects, static fields) but each has its own stack, program counter, and local variables. Benefits: parallelism on multi-core CPUs, responsive UIs, efficient I/O handling, and better resource utilisation. The core risk: shared mutable state — concurrent reads and writes without coordination cause race conditions, stale data, and corruption. Java's concurrency tools — synchronized, volatile, Executor framework, CompletableFuture, and concurrent collections — address these risks.

items.q: What is the difference between Thread class and Runnable interface in Java?
items.a: Thread is a class — extending it creates a thread but uses the single inheritance slot. Runnable is a functional interface with a single void run() method — implementing it separates the task from thread lifecycle, allows extending another class, and is compatible with thread pools and executors. Preference: always implement Runnable (or Callable for results) over extending Thread. Submit Runnables to ExecutorService rather than creating raw Threads — this provides thread reuse, lifecycle management, and rejection handling.

items.q: What is the difference between synchronized method and synchronized block?
items.a: A synchronized method acquires the monitor lock on 'this' (instance) or Class (static) for the entire method. A synchronized block acquires a lock on a specified object for only the block's duration. Synchronized blocks are preferred: smaller critical section = less contention = higher throughput. You can choose any object as the lock — enabling independent locks for independent data, allowing concurrent access to unrelated fields.

items.q: What is a deadlock in Java? How do you prevent it?
items.a: Deadlock: two or more threads permanently blocked, each holding a lock the other needs. Prevention: (1) Lock ordering — always acquire multiple locks in the same global order across all threads (breaks circular wait). (2) tryLock with timeout — ReentrantLock.tryLock(timeout) releases held locks if all can't be acquired (breaks hold-and-wait). (3) Avoid nested locking — minimise holding multiple locks simultaneously. (4) Use high-level concurrency utilities (ConcurrentHashMap, BlockingQueue) that handle locking internally. Detect with jstack or VisualVM thread dump.

items.q: What are virtual threads in Java 21?
items.a: Virtual threads (JEP 444, Java 21) are JVM-managed lightweight threads not backed 1:1 by OS threads. Traditional platform threads cost 1–2MB each; virtual threads start at a few KB. The JVM mounts virtual threads on carrier threads and unmounts them during blocking I/O — allowing millions of concurrent virtual threads. Ideal for: high-concurrency I/O-bound workloads (HTTP servers, database access, REST APIs). Not for: CPU-bound work (no parallelism benefit) or heavily synchronized code doing blocking I/O (pinning). Create with: Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() or Thread.startVirtualThread(runnable).
